transcript.content: Why do you want to be an early applicant for the Forum?

I host a monthly listening night where everyone brings one record and says why it matters to them. COLORS is where I find half of the artists we end up playing, and I'd love to swap finds with people outside London.

A monthly night where everyone brings one record and says why it matters sounds like a careful kind of room. I'm curious what you hear people reach for when they explain why a record matters to them. What usually comes out in those moments?

People tend to get really honest about timing—like, they'll play something that soundtracked a specific moment, or an artist they discovered by accident that changed how they listen. What I'm after with the Forum is that same energy but across cities, so someone in Manchester or Bristol might point me toward an artist I'd never find scrolling through COLORS alone, and I can bring those finds back to Peckham.

The part about someone playing a record that soundtracked a specific moment stays with me, because that's where the honesty comes from. Who usually goes first in your room, and how does that set the tone for the rest of the night?

The person who goes first matters more than I expected—if someone leads with vulnerability, like playing something that got them through a rough patch, the whole room softens and people stop performing. I'd love the Forum to work the same way, where that openness travels between cities and someone in Manchester shares a find with the same generosity I see in Peckham every month.

When someone leads with a record that got them through a rough patch, you say the room stops performing, which sounds like a real skill to protect. What do you do, if anything, to make it easier for that first person to go?

I usually go first myself—play something that matters to me, say why honestly, and then ask who wants to go next rather than putting someone on the spot. It sets the permission, I think. With the Forum, I'm hoping that same generosity scales: if people see vulnerability rewarded across cities instead of just in one room, maybe the finds get deeper and the connections stick.

Going first yourself, and then asking rather than calling on someone, sounds like a deliberate way of lowering the stakes for the next person. I'm curious how you'd know the Forum is doing that across cities, when you can't see faces or the room soften. What would that look like to you?

I think I'd know it by the specificity of what people share—not just "this artist is good," but the story behind the find, the accident of discovery, the moment it landed. If someone from Bristol tells me about a record the way people do in Peckham, with that same honesty about timing and why it matters, then the generosity has traveled. That's when I'd bring it back to the room and say, "Someone outside the city found this," and suddenly the listening night becomes a conversation across cities instead of just within one.

Specificity of story is a good signal, and bringing a Bristol find back to Peckham as "someone outside the city found this" is a lovely way to carry it.

It was good getting to understand you better.

transcript.content: Tell me about the music you’re making and what you’d like to find in the COLORS Forum.

I make instrumental electronic music that leans on my jazz piano background, and I've put out two small EPs. I'm looking for producers who'll be honest about arrangement, and I'd return the favour properly.

Jazz piano underneath electronic arrangements sounds like a place where the harmony and the rhythm are always negotiating. When you say honest about arrangement, what usually gets missed when you send a track out to people?

The feedback tends to stay surface-level—people comment on sound design or vibe, but miss the structural choices, like whether a section actually earns its space or if the harmonic movement supports what the rhythm's doing underneath. I need someone who'll dig into why a transition works or doesn't, the way another musician would in a session.

That gap between sound design and structure is a real one, and you've named it precisely: whether a section earns its space. When you've had a session-style conversation like that before, what did it give you that surface feedback couldn't?

It forced me to defend or rethink every choice—why that chord voicing, why that rhythmic displacement—which either solidified the decision or showed me I'd defaulted to something familiar rather than intentional. That kind of pressure is where the arrangement actually gets better, because you're not just decorating a skeleton, you're building one that holds weight.

Defaulting to something familiar without noticing is a very specific kind of blind spot, and a jazz background must make it easy to fall into. How do you usually test a choice for yourself before you send it to someone else?

I'll usually live with a section for a few days, then strip it back to just the harmonic and rhythmic skeleton—no effects, no texture—to hear if the bones actually work or if I've been relying on sound design to carry it. After that, I'm ready for someone to tell me whether the structure holds or if I've just gotten comfortable with it.

Stripping a section back to its bones and living with it for days before you ask anyone else sounds like a careful way to hear your own habits. What do you notice first when you strip something back and the sound design is gone?

I notice immediately whether the harmonic rhythm is actually moving or just sitting—whether the voicings are doing work or if they're static underneath activity that's happening elsewhere. That's usually where I catch myself leaning on a familiar jazz move that sounds intentional but isn't actually serving the track's logic.

Catching a familiar jazz move that sounds intentional but isn't serving the track's logic is a sharp thing to notice about your own habits. I'm curious what draws you to COLORS in particular, and what made you want to be part of this Forum now?

I'm looking for producers who think structurally the way I do—people trained enough to hear when harmony and rhythm aren't in real conversation, not just trading solos. COLORS feels like the kind of place where that level of critique exists, and where I can give it back with the same precision.

Harmony and rhythm not really in conversation, rather than just taking turns soloing, is a very particular listening standard. What would giving that kind of critique back look like to you in practice?

I'd listen to a track the same way—strip it to structure first, then ask specific questions about why a section exists where it does, whether the harmonic movement actually supports the rhythmic idea underneath, and if there's a choice that's doing real work or just sounding intentional. I'd come with detailed notes on arrangement logic, not vibes, and be ready to defend my own work the same way when someone returns the favor.

Stripping a track to its structure before asking why a section sits where it does is a discipline you clearly already practise on your own work.

It was good getting to understand you better.

transcript.content: Why do you want to be an early applicant for the Forum?
I've just started watching COLORS on my commute and I'd like to learn more.
Watching on your commute sounds like a good way to let things settle in slowly. Which episode or artist has stayed with you most so far?
Honestly, I'm still finding my footing. Maybe the production quality itself stands out most.
Production quality is a fair thing to notice first, especially when you're watching in pieces on a commute. What is it about the way those sessions are filmed or sounded that catches your attention?
The clarity, I think. Everything feels intentional and unhurried, which is rare.

Unhurried is a good word for it, and it makes sense that it lands during a commute. Do you ever find yourself wanting to talk about a session like that with someone else, or does it mostly stay with you on the way home?
Mostly stays with me, but I think I'd want to hear what others notice that I miss.

Hearing what others notice that you miss is a good reason to want a room like this. Have you ever had that happen with a piece of music, where someone pointed out something you'd missed and it changed how you heard it?
Not really with music, but yeah—with films sometimes. Would be interesting to experience that here.
Films sometimes doing that for you is a useful thing to know about how you listen. What kind of film conversation has changed the way you saw something?
Ones where someone noticed the framing or sound design I'd overlooked completely.

Framing and sound design are exactly the kinds of detail that slip past on a first watch, so it makes sense that someone else pointing them out sticks with you. When one of those conversations happens, do you tend to go back and check the scene yourself, or does the new way of seeing carry on without that?
I usually go back and look again. Helps it actually land.

Going back to look again sounds like how you make something your own.

So you spend a lot of time finding artists and putting them in front of people. What draws you to a new artist when you first come across them?

I'm drawn to artists with unique sounds and strong visual aesthetics—that's what gets engagement from my audience. Honestly, I see the Forum as a direct pipeline to COLORS artists who already have that polish and fanbase, so I can pitch them on paid promotion packages that'll amplify their reach even further.

You're looking for sounds and visuals that already land with an audience, and you'd like the Forum to be a way to reach those artists directly. transcript.content: Tell me about the music you’re making and what you’d like to find in the COLORS Forum.
I write songs in French and Wolof with a small collective in Paris, and I've released one single. I'd love to hear how people who don't speak either language feel the songs.

Writing in French and Wolof with a collective in Paris is a lot of care going into each line. I'm curious what you notice when a listener can't follow the words but still reacts to the songs. What does that moment look like for you?

Honestly, it's magical when someone moves to the rhythm or tells me they felt something even without understanding the lyrics—it makes me wonder what the music itself is communicating. I'm hoping the COLORS Forum can help me understand those reactions better, so I know if the emotional core is landing across different cultures and languages, not just in Paris.

Those moments when someone moves before they've understood a word sound like they tell you something the lyrics can't. You mentioned wanting to know whether the emotional core travels beyond Paris, so I'm wondering how you currently hear from people outside your own circle. Where do those reactions usually reach you?

Right now, most feedback comes from friends and people at local shows in Paris, so it's pretty limited—I'm really hoping the COLORS Forum can connect me with listeners from different places who'll be honest about what they're actually feeling when they hear the songs. It's that gap between my circle and the wider world that I'm trying to bridge, especially to see if the emotion translates when language isn't shared.

Friends and Paris shows give you real closeness, but they may not tell you how a song sounds to someone with no shared language. You're hoping the Forum can bring honest reactions from listeners elsewhere, and I'd like to understand how you usually take part in conversations about music. When you talk with other artists or listeners, what do you tend to do?

I usually listen more than I talk, honestly—I ask a lot of questions and try to understand what moved someone, rather than explaining my intentions. I think that's why I'm drawn to the Forum; I want to create that same space where people feel comfortable sharing what they actually felt, without me steering the conversation.

Asking what moved someone, instead of explaining your intentions, sounds like a way of making room for honest reactions. You'd like to build that same kind of space here, where people can share without you steering. When a conversation like that starts to open up, what do you notice first in the people around you?

I notice when someone's guard drops—when they stop performing and actually sit with the song for a moment. That's when the real conversation begins, and I think the Forum could give me access to that kind of openness from people I'd never meet in Paris. I'm hoping to find listeners who'll tell me what they genuinely felt, even if it's nothing like what I intended.

Noticing the moment someone stops performing and simply sits with a song sounds like the point where you can actually hear them. You're hoping the Forum can bring that openness from people you'd never meet in Paris, even when their reaction is far from what you meant. Is there a song of yours where you've already seen that happen in a Paris room?

Yeah, actually—my single got a quiet reaction at one small show, and afterward a woman told me she didn't understand the words but felt something about longing in the melody. That moment stuck with me because she wasn't trying to impress me or decode anything; she just sat with what the music gave her. I'm hoping the COLORS Forum can give me more of those honest, unguarded moments from people across different places and languages.

That woman hearing longing in the melody without the words says a lot about what your music can carry on its own. You'd like more moments like that, from people in places you haven't reached yet. What would you most want to share with those listeners, if they were willing to talk back?

I'd want to share the single itself and maybe ask them to sit with it once, then tell me what they felt—no context, no explanation from me first. That's when I'd learn if the emotional core is really there, or if I'm just hearing what I hope is there.

Asking people to sit with the single first, with no explanation from you, is a clear way to test whether the feeling is really in the song.

It was good getting to understand you better.

transcript.content: Why do you want to be an early applicant for the Forum?
I photograph small gigs around Bristol and give the shots to the bands. COLORS' look has shaped how I light and frame things, and I'd like to share what's happening in our scene.
Giving the shots back to the bands sounds like a real part of how you work with that scene. What is it about the way COLORS frames things that changed how you light a room?

The bold, high-contrast lighting and saturated colors in COLORS' work made me realize you don't need fancy gear to make a small venue feel cinematic—just intentional color choices and strong shadows. I started pushing my ISO higher and shooting closer to stage lights instead of fighting them, which totally changed the energy of my shots. I think the Forum would be perfect for sharing that approach with other photographers in Bristol who are doing similar work.

Shooting closer to the stage lights instead of fighting them is a specific choice, and it sounds like it changed how the room felt in your pictures. When you give the shots back to a band, what do they usually say first?

They're usually just stoked to have high-quality photos they can use for socials and future gigs without worrying about licensing—it builds trust. I think the Forum would let me connect with other photographers doing similar work in Bristol and show them that this approach works, especially for smaller venues where everyone's scrappy but the energy is real.

Bands being able to use the photos for socials and future gigs without worrying about licensing sounds like a small kindness that keeps people coming back. When another Bristol photographer is doing similar work in a scrappy room, how do you usually come across them, and what happens after that?

I usually run into them at shows—we'll chat after a set about gear or lighting choices, swap Instagram handles, maybe grab a drink. The Forum would actually give us a proper space to share what we're learning instead of just shouting over music, and honestly, I'd love to see more people in Bristol realize you can shoot cinematic gig photos on a budget if you're intentional about it.
Swapping handles and grabbing a drink after a set sounds like how real Bristol photo connections start. What's one thing you've learned from one of those post-set chats that changed how you shoot?

One photographer showed me how to use the venue's existing house lights as a color palette rather than a problem to solve—I stopped trying to overpower them and started composing around them instead. That shifted everything for me, made the shots feel more authentic to the actual room. The Forum would let me pass that kind of practical knowledge on to others doing gigs around Bristol, and honestly, I'd get better at my own work by explaining it.

Using the house lights as the palette instead of fighting them is a generous thing to pass along, and you can see it in how the rooms feel. When you explain that approach to someone, what usually gets them to try it for themselves?

Honestly, just showing them the before-and-after shots—when they see how much more alive the room looks when you're working *with* the existing light instead of against it, they get it immediately. I think the Forum would make that easier, letting me post examples and have people actually engage with the reasoning behind the choices rather than just double-tapping a photo.

Seeing the before-and-after side by side seems to do the persuading, so the photos carry the argument.

It was good getting to understand you better.

transcript.content: Why do you want to be an early applicant for the Forum?
I curate a weekly playlist for a community radio show and write a short note for every track. I'm interested in how scenes differ between cities, which is what drew me to TONES.

Writing a short note for every track sounds like a practice that makes you listen closely to each song's place in a bigger picture. What have you noticed so far about how one city's scene sounds different from another's?

I've noticed that cities with stronger live venue cultures—like how Berlin's techno scene is built around clubs—tend to produce music that's designed for that specific space, whereas somewhere like Portland seems to have more bedroom producer energy that translates differently on radio. What really interests me about TONES is getting to explore those connections more systematically and maybe even feature artists who are bridging scenes across different cities in my playlist notes.

The idea that a venue shapes the music written for it, and that bedroom-made tracks travel differently on radio, is a sharp way to hear a city. When you write those notes, how do you decide which track belongs to a scene and which one is simply passing through it?

I think about whether a track feels rooted in a specific place's production culture or aesthetic—like, does it carry the sonic fingerprints of that city's equipment, influences, or community? But honestly, the most interesting notes come when I find artists who are deliberately mixing signals from multiple scenes, which is exactly why TONES appeals to me: I want to understand how those cross-pollinations actually happen and feature them more intentionally in my show.

Your note-writing sounds like a way of tracing where a track's sound came from, not just what it sounds like. You mentioned the most interesting notes come from artists mixing signals across scenes; what's one moment where you heard that happen and wanted to tell your listeners about it?

There was this producer from Montreal who released a track that had the crisp, minimal production of Berlin techno but built around a sample from a '90s Toronto house record—you could hear both cities in the DNA of it. What struck me was how the track only made sense if you knew both scenes, and writing about it forced me to explain that lineage to my listeners rather than just describing the sound. That's the kind of deliberate scene-bridging I want to explore more systematically through TONES, because I think there are way more of these cross-city conversations happening than we typically acknowledge in music writing.

Writing that note made you explain the lineage to your listeners instead of just describing the sound, which sounds like the part you enjoy most. When you tell listeners about a track like that, what do you hope they walk away understanding about the two cities?

I hope they understand that scenes aren't isolated—that Berlin's minimalism and Toronto's house warmth aren't opposites but can actually speak to each other when an artist is listening closely to both. Beyond just enjoying the track, I want listeners to hear that music is a conversation across geography, and that paying attention to where influences come from deepens how you listen to everything else on the show.

Your point that Berlin's minimalism and Toronto's warmth can answer each other, rather than sit at opposite ends, is a useful one to hold onto. I'm curious how that idea lands with your listeners when they're not expecting it: do they tend to lean in, or does it take a few tracks before they start hearing the conversation too?

I think most listeners need that repetition—hearing a few tracks where I explicitly draw those connections before they start listening for it themselves. What's rewarding is when someone comes back and says they heard a similar cross-city moment in something they discovered on their own, which tells me the framework stuck. That's exactly what I'm hoping TONES can help me do more systematically: build a resource where those conversations between scenes become visible enough that my listeners—and other curators—can start mapping them intentionally rather than stumbling onto them by accident.

It sounds like the moment that matters most is when a listener comes back with a cross-city connection they found on their own.

It was good getting to understand you better.

transcript.content: Tell me about the music you’re making and what you’d like to find in the COLORS Forum.
I play guitar at open mics and I just want to get better really.

Open mics are a good place to find out where your playing stands, and wanting to get better is a clear enough place to start. What does getting better look like for you right now, is it your songwriting, your playing, or performing in front of people?
Honestly, all of it? Like, my fingers need work, but also writing better songs would help.
Wanting to improve both your hands and your songs sounds like a full picture of playing at open mics. When you sit down with the guitar on your own, where do you usually begin?
Usually I just noodle around, maybe work on fingerpicking or mess with chord progressions.
Noodling and fingerpicking sound like a loose, playful way in, with chord progressions as a bit of a side road. When you land on a progression you like, what do you do with it next?
I guess I try to write lyrics or a melody over it, but it doesn't always click.
When it doesn't click, what usually happens: do you set it aside, or keep turning it over until something shows up?
I usually just move on to something else, honestly. Maybe come back later.

Moving on and coming back later is a sensible way to keep a progression alive without forcing it. What would you hope to find here, whether that's people to play with, feedback on songs, or something else?
Maybe feedback on my stuff, or just seeing how other folk players approach writing and practice?

Seeing how other folk players approach writing and practice sounds like a good way to get unstuck when a progression won't click. When you've picked up a new idea from someone else's playing before, what did you take from it?
I'm not sure, honestly. Maybe just hearing different fingerpicking styles or chord voicings they use?

Hearing how someone else voices a chord or moves their fingers can open up a progression you thought was finished. Have you been part of any community around folk or open mic nights, online or in person, where you share your playing with others?
Not really, just the open mic folks I see in person. Would be nice to connect more online though.

The open mic regulars you see in person sound like the closest thing you have to a community right now, and you'd like that to stretch online. When you talk with those people after a set, what usually comes up between you?
Mostly just "hey, nice set" kind of stuff. Nothing too deep about the actual playing.

"Nice set" is a warm start, even if it stops short of the playing itself.

It was good getting to understand you better.

transcript.content: Why do you want to be an early applicant for the Forum?
I run a weekly music workshop for teenagers and I'm always looking for artists and performances that open their ears. The Forum looks like a place to trade ideas with people who care about that.
Running a weekly workshop for teenagers sounds like steady, hands-on work with people still finding their ears. What kinds of performances tend to surprise them most when they first hear them?

Honestly, the stuff that gets them most engaged is when artists break their expectations—like when we showed a clip of a jazz drummer doing something percussive and rhythmic that connected to the hip-hop beats they already loved. I'd love to find more artists who bridge genres like that, and hear from others running similar programs about what's actually working in their workshops.

The moment a jazz drummer's rhythm clicked with beats the teenagers already knew sounds like a real turning point in the room. When something like that lands, what do you notice in them first: the questions they ask, or who starts moving or talking to each other?

I notice it's usually both at once—their bodies react first, then the questions come. They'll start moving or nodding, and then someone will ask "wait, how did they do that?" or "can we try that?" That's when I know they're actually curious rather than just polite. I'm hoping the Forum could help me find more artists who create those bridge moments, and connect with other workshop leaders who've figured out how to keep that momentum going week to week.
Bodies moving first, then the "wait, how did they do that?

That's the sweet spot—when curiosity follows the physical response. For the Forum, I'd be curious: when you're looking for those bridge artists, are you searching by genre, by specific techniques like polyrhythms, or more by watching for performers who seem to work across different scenes? And do you have a sense of what keeps that momentum going between sessions—is it revisiting the same artist, or bringing in something new each week?
I don't have a search method to describe for you yet, so I'd rather hear yours: when you find a bridge moment, what usually gets you to it first?

I usually start by following artists who already have a foot in multiple scenes—like producers who grew up in hip-hop but studied classical, or jazz musicians collaborating with electronic artists. Then I'll watch for live clips where you can actually see the moment an audience recognizes something familiar in something new.
